column10: `rule.fired = true` mutates the TriggerRule object in place. `loadScenario` registers the same object references from `ScenarioData` directly (no copy). If `ScenarioData` is a module-level singleton (as `villagerBasicScenario` is), `fired` state bleeds across multiple game rooms or test runs that load the same scenario. Any `once: true` trigger that fires in one room will appear already-fired in the next room loaded from that singleton.

`extractFactKeys` only traverses `fact_ref` nodes. Trigger conditions that reference only `prop_ref` (e.g., `$npc.hp < 10`), `local_ref`, or builtin `call` nodes without any `fact_ref` subexpressions produce an empty `deps` set. An empty `deps` means no key in `changedFacts` can ever match, so `relevant` is always false and those triggers silently never evaluate, regardless of whether their condition is met.

The `EvalContext` used for trigger condition evaluation stubs out `player` and `npc` accessors to always return `0`. Any trigger `when` expression using `has_item("$player", ...)`, `faction_of("$npc")`, `distance("$player", "$npc")`, or `prop_ref` against player/npc silently evaluates those sub-expressions as `0` instead of the actual agent state. This causes triggers to fire or not fire incorrectly without any error.

Phase 8 trigger execution only handles `set_fact` effects; `give_item`, `take_item`, `damage`, and `register_trigger` emit a console.warn and are dropped silently. The DSL allows all these effect types on triggers (they're in the `Effect` union), they serialize and load without error, and the executor in `executor.ts` correctly handles them — but the tick loop's trigger execution path simply ignores them. Authors who write triggers with item or damage effects will get no runtime error and no functional behaviour.

`register()` throws on duplicate IDs. The `register_trigger` effect in an action node passes `effect.trigger` (a fixed object reference with a fixed `id`) to `this.triggerRegistry?.register(rule)` in `DialogueSession.buildMutableContext()`. If a dialogue tree loops back to an action node containing a `register_trigger` effect (e.g., `node A → choice → back to A`), the second visit throws `Duplicate trigger rule id`, which propagates uncaught through `executeEffects` → `advanceWithEffects` → `getState()`, crashing the session.

`currentTick` is captured once at session construction and never updated. Beliefs written via `setFact` during a session are stamped with the construction tick (line 173: `tick: this.currentTick`). For sessions that span multiple server ticks — which is inevitable when awaiting an LLM response on a `request` node — those beliefs get a stale timestamp. Other agents' beliefs for the same key with higher (more-recent) ticks will overwrite them during belief merges, even though the dialogue-set belief was actually more recent.

`build()` validates that text nodes have a non-empty `next` field but does not validate that any referenced node IDs (`next`, `nextYes`, `nextNo`, option `next`) actually exist in the `nodes` map. Typos in `goto()`, `nextYes`/`nextNo`, or manually-specified `next` targets are silently accepted at build time and only raise an error at runtime when `DialogueEngine.getCurrentNode()` throws `Dialogue node "..." not found`.

The recursive call in `getState()` to auto-advance through `action` nodes can lead to a stack overflow if there's a long chain of such nodes. While a depth limit of 100 is implemented to prevent infinite loops, a large but finite chain could still exceed Node.js's stack depth limit. The function should be converted to an iterative loop to handle arbitrarily long chains of action nodes without consuming stack space.

During trigger evaluation, all agents' beliefs are merged into a single `allBeliefs` map. This creates a global view of all facts, which violates the project's design principle of "no global omniscience". Triggers should be evaluated against an agent's local knowledge (their own beliefs and those of adjacent agents they have merged with), not a world-state view. This gives agents with access to more information an unfair advantage and leaks information across the map.

When a trigger fires and applies a `set_fact` effect, the `evaluate` call to resolve the fact's value is provided with a limited `EvalContext` that does not include full agent or settlement state. The context is hardcoded with accessors that return 0 for most properties, which will lead to incorrect calculations for any expression that relies on agent state (like HP, position, or inventory other than what's held by the target agent). This breaks triggers that need to compute new facts based on the state of the world.

The `mergeBeliefs` method creates a shallow copy of each fact using the spread syntax (`{ ...fact }`). If a fact's `value` is an object or array, it will not be deep-copied. While `Value` is currently defined as `boolean | number | string`, this creates a risk of shared mutable state if complex fact values are introduced in the future, as two agents could then hold references to the same mutable object within their belief stores.

When constructing a `DialogueSession`, the `locals` from a pre-existing `DialogueProgressEntry` are loaded. However, `visitedNodes` and `selectedOptions` are ignored. This means that if a conversation is resumed, the dialogue engine will not remember which nodes have been seen or which choices were made, potentially allowing players to re-trigger one-time options or see different conditional paths than they should.

The `evaluateDialogueGate` function, which asks an LLM to decide on a player's request, constructs a `makeAccessor` for agent properties but only exposes the agent's inventory, not other properties like HP or position. When interpolating the request label, any `prop_ref` to non-inventory properties (e.g., `t`Your HP is ${npc.prop('hp')}`t`) will incorrectly resolve to 0.

The `div` operation in the arithmetic evaluator returns 0 when dividing by zero. This can silently produce incorrect results in calculations (e.g., `100 / 0` becomes `0` instead of indicating an error). It would be safer to throw an error or return `NaN` to make division-by-zero errors more visible and prevent them from propagating as valid-looking numbers.

The `evaluateBatch` method does not handle errors if `checkCondition` throws, potentially leaving `fired` rules in inconsistent states. This could disrupt the proper execution of conditional triggers.
In `giveItem`, if the target agent's inventory does not exist, no error is raised, and the operation silently fails. This behavior can mask problems in agent setup or data integrity.
In `takeItem`, there is no validation if the agent's inventory does not exist, and failures return false. This could lead to unclear error handling logic depending on the caller's behavior.
`advanceWithEffects` does not check for improperly defined action nodes without effects, leading to potential runtime errors or undefined behaviors.
`loadScenario` directly sets agent beliefs during NPC creation without any validation or deduplication checks. This behavior could allow conflicting data entries or duplicate beliefs.
Beliefs are converted to strings using `String(fact.value)`, which may fail for non-primitive values and could lead to unexpected results if any value is an object or a non-string data type.
`selectOption` throws an error if an out-of-range index is selected. While exceptions might be helpful during development, bounds checking or user feedback mechanisms would better fit production.

[javascript.lang.security.audit.unsafe-formatstring.unsafe-formatstring] Detected string concatenation with a non-literal variable in a util.format / console.log function. If an attacker injects a format specifier in the string, it will forge the log message. Try to use constant values for the format string.

Phase 8 trigger evaluation depends on `recordChangedFact` being called when beliefs change, but `recordChangedFact` is only invoked from `DialogueSession.setFact` (see `dialogue-session.ts:174`). The other paths that mutate beliefs — `Agent.setBelief` called from `scenario-loader.ts:30`, `Agent.mergeBeliefs` called from `vision.ts:58-59` during phase 7, and the trigger's own `targetAgent.setBelief(...)` at line 209 below — never record changes. As a result, scenario-level triggers will essentially never fire from normal gameplay (belief merges between adjacent agents won't trigger anything), and triggers that themselves modify facts won't cause downstream triggers to fire on the next tick. Consider routing belief mutations through a helper that records the change, or have `Agent.setBelief`/`mergeBeliefs` accept an optional `TriggerRegistry` to record into.

`loadScenario` returns a `triggerRegistry` but does not assign it to `state.triggerRegistry`. Since `processTick` only evaluates triggers when `state.triggerRegistry` is set (see `tick.ts:161`), callers have to remember to do `state.triggerRegistry = loadScenario(...).triggerRegistry` manually, otherwise the entire trigger system is silently inert. Consider either assigning it inside `loadScenario` (since the loader is already mutating `state.agents`), or returning a result that makes the wiring explicit.

`getState` is named like a read-only accessor but, on `action` nodes, it calls `engine.advanceWithEffects(...)` which mutates engine state and executes side effects (set_fact, give_item, etc.) before recursing. Calling `getState()` twice in a row on the same session can therefore yield different results and re-trigger effects already applied (well, the second call would land on a non-action node so effects wouldn't re-run, but the implicit advance still happens once). At minimum the name and JSDoc should make the mutating behavior obvious; better would be to do the auto-advance only on explicit `advance()`/`select()`/`resolveRequest()` transitions and have `getState()` return the raw current node (possibly throwing or skipping if the engine is parked on an action node).

`loadScenario` creates and returns a `TriggerRegistry` but never attaches it to `state.triggerRegistry`, while `processTick` only evaluates triggers from `state.triggerRegistry`. Since this function otherwise mutates the provided state when spawning NPCs, callers that simply load a scenario will get no Phase 8 trigger execution unless they remember an extra assignment.

Initial beliefs are inserted directly on the agent without recording the changed fact keys in the trigger registry. `TriggerRegistry.evaluateBatch` skips every rule whose dependency is not in `changedFacts`, so scenario triggers that should fire from facts present at spawn time will never run.

Beliefs learned through adjacency are not reported to the trigger registry. Because Phase 8 filters rules using `changedFacts`, a trigger depending on a fact propagated by `mergeBeliefs` will be skipped even though the target agent's beliefs changed this tick.

Facts written by trigger effects are not recorded as changed facts. Since the registry clears `changedFacts` at the end of the tick and only evaluates rules whose dependencies are marked changed, triggers cannot chain from facts produced by other triggers on the next tick.

The effect's own `target` is ignored here; every `set_fact` effect is applied to each trigger target being iterated. For example, a rule with `targets: ["elder", "scout"]` and `setFact("elder", ...)` will write the fact to both elder and scout, which changes the authored semantics of the effect.

Trigger targets only resolve concrete agent IDs in this branch. The shared `AgentRef` type and DSL allow `$player`/`$npc`, but those refs fall through to `agents.get("$player")`/`agents.get("$npc")` and are skipped, so valid trigger targets never receive their effects.

This serializes every belief into the LLM prompt with no cap or prioritization, unlike memories which are limited to five entries. As belief stores grow through propagation and triggers, prompts can become unexpectedly large and hit model/context or latency limits.

Registering a node with an ID that already exists silently overwrites the previous node while leaving the old entry in `nodeOrder`. A typo or duplicate ID can change the dialogue root/links without any build-time error, producing a tree that fails later at runtime.

The `text()` API accepts `opts.context`, but the builder never stores it in `DialogueNodeData` or passes it to locale resolution. Authors can provide a disambiguation context that is silently discarded, so localized text using `@@context` cannot work for these nodes.

`give_item` accepts any JavaScript number, including negative, `NaN`, or `Infinity`. Because `Agent.addToInventory` directly adds the amount, a negative or non-finite scripted amount can corrupt inventory instead of being rejected.

`take_item` only checks that the evaluated amount is a number, so negative or non-finite amounts are forwarded to inventory removal. With the current `Agent.removeFromInventory` implementation, a negative take increases the target's inventory instead of deducting resources.

`damage` accepts negative and non-finite numbers. A negative scripted damage amount is passed to `Agent.takeDamage`, which subtracts it and can heal the target above its maximum HP instead of applying damage.

Dialogue action effects can be authored with any `AgentRef` (including concrete agent IDs and `$faction:*`), but session execution only resolves `$npc` and `$player`. A valid scripted effect such as `setFact("elder", ...)` will throw at runtime when reached in dialogue.

`getData()` returns the option builder's mutable backing object, and this code mutates/stores that same object in the tree. If an `OptionBuilder` is accidentally reused in another choice, the later `data.id` assignment mutates the option already stored on the earlier choice.
